The reason we train is to get better.

Every successful product goes from version 1.0 to 2.0, eventually.

Very few people still drive a Model T.

It’s not perfect, not yet. But we ship the work because it’s on the way to the next step.

Perfect isn’t possible. Better always is.

# The Art of Being Alone: May Sarton’s Stunning 1938 Ode to Solitude

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 33: The Art of Being Alone: May Sarton’s Stunning 1938 Ode to Solitude](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/innerlandscape_maysarton.jpg?fit=320%2C488&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Inner-Landscape-Poems-May-Sarton/dp/1684220084/?tag=braipick-20)

_“The best things in life happen to you when you’re alone,”_ artist Agnes Martin [reflected](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/03/22/agnes-martin-1997-interview/) in her final years. _“Oh comforting solitude, how favorable thou art to original thought!”_ wrote the founding father of neuroscience in his [advice to young scientists](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/04/20/cajal-science-solitude/). The poet Elizabeth Bishop [believed](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/08/elizabeth-bishop-solitude/) that everyone should experience at least one prolonged period of solitude in life. For in true solitude, as Wendell Berry [so memorably observed](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/12/17/wendell-berry-pride-despair-solitude/), “one’s inner voices become audible [and] in consequence, one responds more clearly to other lives” — an intuitive understanding of what psychologists have since found: that [“fertile solitude”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/07/18/adam-phillips-on-risk-and-solitude/) is the basic unit of a full and contented life.

But in the neutral state of aloneness, the psychoemotional line between solitude and loneliness can be as thin as a razor’s edge and as lacerating to the soul. How to draw it skillfully in orienting ourselves to the world, exterior and interior, is what poet, novelist, and memoirist **May Sarton** (May 3, 1912–July 16, 1995) explores in a beautiful poem she penned ten days after her twenty-sixth birthday, decades before she came to contemplate solitude in [stunning prose](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/10/17/may-sarton-journal-of-a-solitude-depression/). Originally titled “Considerations,” the poem was slightly revised and published the following year as “Canticle 6” in Sarton’s second poetry collection, the altogether sublime [**_Inner Landscape_**](https://www.amazon.com/Inner-Landscape-Poems-May-Sarton/dp/1684220084/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/inner-landscape-poems/oclc/503703214&referer=brief_results)).

> **CANTICLE 6**  
> _by May Sarton_
> 
> 
> Alone one is never lonely: the spirit  
> adventures, waking  
>  In a quiet garden, in a cool house, abiding single there;  
>  The spirit adventures in sleep, the sweet thirst-slaking  
>  When only the moon’s reflection touches the wild hair.  
>  There is no place more intimate than the spirit alone:  
>  It finds a lovely certainty in the evening and the morning.  
>  It is only where two have come together bone against bone  
>  That those alonenesses take place, when, without warning  
>  The sky opens over their heads to an infinite hole in space;  
>  It is only turning at night to a lover that one learns  
>  He is set apart like a star forever and that sleeping face  
>  (For whom the heart has cried, for whom the frail hand burns)  
>  Is swung out in the night alone, so luminous and still,  
>  The waking spirit attends, the loving spirit gazes  
>  Without communion, without touch, and comes to know at last  
>  Out of a silence only and never when the body blazes  
>  That love is present, that always burns alone, however steadfast.

Complement with Louise Bourgeois on [how solitude enriches creative work](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/04/15/louise-bourgeois-solitude/), Virginia Woolf on [the relationship between loneliness and creativity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/06/16/virginia-woolf-loneliness/), and Olivia Laing’s [masterwork on the art of being alone](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/07/11/the-lonely-city-olivia-laing/), then revisit other readings of beautiful poems of existential radiance: Derek Walcott’s [“Love After Love,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/04/21/love-after-love-derek-walcott/) Wisława Szymborska’s [“Life-While-You-Wait,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/07/02/amanda-palmer-reads-wislawa-szymborska/) Jane Kenyon’s [“Having It Out With Melancholy,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/09/27/having-it-out-with-melancholy-jane-kenyon-amanda-palmer/) and Adrienne Rich’s [“Planetarium.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/04/27/janna-levin-reads-planetarium-by-adrienne-rich/)

# Meteor of Joy: The Young People’s Chorus of New York City Sings Bird Divinations

### By Maria Popova

Children know the deepest truths about life, the elemental knowledge we unlearn in the act of living, those inarticulable truths music alone helps us remember. To hear children sing the secret wisdom of the heart is to be in the presence of something truer and more transcendent than any of our poems and postulates can touch — the ultimate affirmation of our aliveness, emanating Richard Powers’s beautiful and bittersweet assertion that [“the use of music is to remind us how short a time we have a body.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/10/15/richard-powers-music/)

To celebrate [twenty years of _The Marginalian_](https://www.youtube.com/live/qKd8UMjQ2Mo), composer extraordinaire [Paola Prestini](https://www.paolaprestini.com/) set six of her favorite [bird divinations](https://almanacofbirds.org/) to music, which the [Young People’s Chorus of New York City](https://ypc.org/) brought to life with their commanding innocence and their tender power. Paola’s perfect title for the piece, drawn from one of the cards, captures what every child is when this world is worth of its children: “Meteor of Joy.”

# Truth, Fact, and the Patterning of Reality: Virginia Woolf on How We Come to Know the World

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 34: Truth, Fact, and the Patterning of Reality: Virginia Woolf on How We Come to Know the World](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/woolf_commonreader.jpg?fit=320%2C488&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Common-Reader-First-Annotated/dp/015602778X/?tag=braipick-20)

The great myth is that truth is an emergent property of fact, that it bubbles up from the bottom of reality once the mind attains enough fathoms of factuality. But [objective reality](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/02/01/niels-bohr-science-religion/) — all those things like gravity and light and the fossil of the Archaeopteryx that exist whether or not we believe in them — is pocked with myriad subjective realities, each lensed through the particular [qualia](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/25/christof-koch-consciousness-qualia/) of the perceiver, each a function not of the mind alone but of the entire organism and the whole of its lived experience, embodied and enacted by the total creature. What we call truth, and how we arrive at it, has more to do with that tessellated totality than with the mind’s rational analysis of reality.

[Virginia Woolf](https://themarginalian.org/tag/virginia-woolf) (January 25, 1882–March 28, 1941) explores this with her characteristic rigor of thought and passion for language in a wonderful essay about the Ancient Greeks later included in [**_The Common Reader_**](https://www.amazon.com/Common-Reader-First-Annotated/dp/015602778X/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/common-reader-first-and-second-series-combined-in-one-volume/oclc/531743868&referer=brief_results)) — the classic collection that also gave us Woolf on [how to hear your soul](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/09/12/virginia-woolf-soul/).

![Image 35](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/virginiawoolf3.jpg?resize=600%2C360&ssl=1)

Virginia Woolf

With an eye to “the indomitable honesty, the courage, the love of truth” that made Socrates such a timeless fulcrum of wisdom (which, I suppose, is the ultimate use of the truth), and in fiery defiance of Descartes, she insists that we arrive at the truth — about the world, about ourselves, about the substance life is made of — with more than the mind:

> What matters is not so much the end we reach as our manner of reaching it… Truth is various; truth comes to us in different disguises; it is not with the intellect alone that we perceive it… Truth is to be pursued with all our faculties. Are we to rule out the amusements, the tendernesses, the frivolities of friendship because we love truth? Will truth be quicker found because we stop our ears to music and drink no wine, and sleep instead of talking through the long winter’s night? It is not to the cloistered disciplinarian mortifying himself in solitude that we are to turn, but to the well-sunned nature, the [man](https://www.themarginalian.org/pronoun/) who practises the art of living to the best advantage, so that nothing is stunted but some things are permanently more valuable than others.

The great paradox is that truth — the truth — is at once multifarious and unitary, something Woolf captures in her altogether exquisite meditation on [creativity as the antipode to the “non-being” that slips over reality like cotton wool](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/09/virginia-woolf-cotton-wool-moments-of-being/), at the end of which she writes:

> Behind the cotton wool is hidden a pattern… The whole world is a work of art [and] we are parts of the work of art. _Hamlet_ or a Beethoven quartet is the truth about this vast mass that we call the world. But there is no Shakespeare, there is no Beethoven; certainly and emphatically there is no God; we are the words; we are the music; we are the thing itself.

# What Is Your Refugium?

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 35: What Is Your Refugium?](https://www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/aforestlanguage-320x448.avif)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/25/a-forest-language-hannah-fries/)

For courage, says Bulgarian folk wisdom instructs, keep a horse chestnut in your pocket.

Even as a child, I was mistrustful of superstition. But every autumn, I would pick up dozens of them from the sidewalks of Sofia and fill my pockets — not as a spell against fear but as an ode to joy. Conkers, as the English call them, spun me up in delight — shiny as mahogany, smooth as river stones, tiny planets from some other universe, the wonder-smitten eyes of some prehistoric creature.

I didn’t know then that they are emblems of life’s irrepressible insistence on itself — miniature monuments to the stubborn creativity of survival.

![Image 36](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/horsechestnut_TheMarginalian.jpg?resize=680%2C888&ssl=1)

Illustration from _Die Baume und Straucher des Waldes_ by by Gustav Hempel and Karl Wilhelm, 1889.

Three million years ago, as the Ice Age was beginning to sink its cool blue fangs into the warm body of Earth, the widespread horse chestnut (_Aesculus hippocastanum_) began dying off, until only a small population remained, most of it sheltered in the gorges of Bulgaria’s mountains. There, in their sanctum of stone, the trees found themselves unable to attract pollinators during the slender three-week window of their flowering.

This is the story of life — innovate or die: The horse chestnut evolved enormous white flower spikes with pink tips and a chemical hack to block the oxidation of polyphenols in the petal, which turns each flower brown and sheds it after pollination. For three whole weeks, the horse chestnut remains a bride in a gown of amazement, its crown an aria of perfect white blossoms that no bee can resist, all because there was a safe place in which to experiment with the possible.

![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/horsechestnut1_TheMarginalian.jpg?resize=680%2C972&ssl=1)

Illustration from _American Medicinal Plants_ by Charles Frederick Millspaugh, 1887.

That place, I learn from my poet friend Hannah Fries’s absolutely wonderful book [_A Forest Language_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/25/a-forest-language-hannah-fries/), is called _refugium_. Hannah writes:

> When glaciers last crept down from the Arctic, 20,000 years ago, there were places where the icy fingers didn’t reach — mountaintops, hot springs, lowlands beyond the ice. There were pockets of green where things crawled and slithered and ate and mated, protected places where life went on, and from which life set forth again as the ice receded. Refugia.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> The gift of a refugium is time. It holds in its small cup of safety a promise for a new world to come. And it lends out to the living all the years, centuries, millennia it might take to finally find that world.
> 
> 
> Even in easier times, it is wise to tend the refuge. What is Earth, after all, but a momentary refugium in the inhospitable blackness of space? From a vantage point far beyond our grasping glows the blue-green dot, a brief and luminous memory in the mind of the universe.
> 
> 
> It is the memory of a place where a simple cell had the ambition to harness the energy of a star, and from it, the green wonder of leaves, the trunks rising up, bursting and blooming into the sky — all of life in the sweet, cool shade below.

We too need them, these refugia that shelter us, that save us in the ice ages of life. Whatever your refugium may be — a place, a person, a practice, a poem — it is worth tending to with all the might and all the means you have.

title: The Sediment Of Culture Shapes Political Order
content:
Credits

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

As a global journal of ideas, Noema receives feedback from readers all over the world that broadens our way of seeing and kindles the further iteration of our thinking. One recent case is a response by Carl Gay, an executive of the Cloudspago consultancy in Australia, to the [Noema](https://www.noemamag.com/when-the-present-eats-the-future/)essay “When The Present Eats The Future: The Achilles Heel of Consumer Democracies.”

In that essay, I contrast post-Mao China’s capacity for reaching a consensus on long-term goals and determinedly implementing them over many years without a break in continuity with the increasing inability of consumer democracies to do so. The example I used in the context of climate change was how China set the goal decades ago of dominating green technology, especially electric vehicles and batteries, and has steadily achieved that objective, while most open societies of the West have sputtered behind. Its “whole dragon” approach brings the resources of the entire system to bear on the challenge at hand.

I pointed out that the strength of China’s system is closely related to its chief flaw:enforcing order and repressing freedom to keep the consensus from fraying. In his note to Noema, Gay makes explicit what I only implied: To the extent China’s determined continuity clogs corrective feedback loops, a policy ordained by the Party can go off in the wrong direction for a very long time, causing damage not easily repaired.

The example he uses is the disastrous one-child policy that held from 1980-2015. It resulted in today’s demographic implosion, where there are not enough young people to sustain the welfare of an aging society. Indeed, blinkered assumptions from the present, projected forward, robbed the future of a balanced population.

Another less calamitous case in point was the 2022 COVID lockdown, which went on well past the patience of a restless public. In that case, the nascent feedback loops of contagious online rants, instances of journalistic exposure and even episodic outbursts of public demonstration resulted in a responsive and more immediate change in policy.

> “Deep culture always returns to shape a society in a way similar to how a person’s emotional subconscious is forever biting at the heels of rational cognition.”

## **The Equivalent Of Market Signals In Politics**

The big question for China’s one-party juggernaut is whether it can accommodate corrective feedback mechanisms in politics that are equivalent to the market signals it accommodates to check state-backed economic policy from going too far down the wrong path.

Two developments are emerging that impact this feedback deficit. Paradoxically, the first is that expanded surveillance from the top serves at the same time to register people’s dissatisfaction to the Party guardians listening at scale.

The other is that China’s densely wired society has become a ready platform for surveillance of official behavior from below, or _sousveillance_. Citizen reports, especially about corruption, rapidly gain virality when posted online.

This dual potential is not lost on the authorities. In a candid conversation in Beijing in 2015, China’s then cyber czar, Lu Wei, openly acknowledged that, in the absence of electoral accountability, an active netizenry can be a critical channel for sending rectifying signals from the grassroots to the Party hierarchy. Even the choice of keyword searches used to invoke censorship can be considered a form of feedback.

Needless to say, if the receiver is not attuned to the signal frequency, the message will go unheard.

Beyond that, a Shanghai entrepreneur I know who was a founder of YouKu, China’s version of YouTube, has told me how the Party is constantly polling down to the neighborhood level to gauge any discontent that may be bubbling up.

China scholar John Keane goes so far as to suggest that China is becoming a kind of “phantom democracy.” By that, he means “the fear of democracy forces a style of political management that in many ways mirrors and mimics electoral systems, where the fear of elections puts leaders in a constant campaign mode” as they feel the need to continually convince constituencies of their worthiness and legitimacy.

But Gay’s key insight in his reply to the Noema essay is more profound and is a larger frame for understanding why China functions as well as it does in contrast to consumer democracies.

> “Culture is the substructure upon which the superstructure of ideology, politics and economics are built — the opposite of how modern thought would have it.”

## **Accumulated Culture Matters Most**

As Gay puts it, “power, ideology and culture run at three speeds. Power changes in years, ideology in decades, culture in generations. China’s ‘whole dragon’ approach works because all three are aligned: a power layer that sets fifty-year goals, an ideology that makes its accountability internal and a culture with two thousand years of examination-system deference deposited in it. The continuity you admire is what alignment produces.

“Consumer democracies have the opposite shape: a return channel for error and no continuity. But ‘a governing consensus that sticks’ is a power-layer prescription, and consensus can’t be installed at the power layer when the culture isn’t carrying it. The rules change; the people don’t. Democracies lack a constituency for the future not because opinion is fickle but because the culture hasn’t yet accumulated the consequences that would create one. It will, when the damage becomes undeniable. That is slower than the climate clock allows, but it’s the only route the mechanism offers.”

Gay expanded on this useful frame elsewhere in an [essay](https://integraloflife.com/article-power-ideology-culture) titled, “Power, Ideology And Culture: The Sediment Beneath Politics.”

“Political order is not one thing but three, moving at three different speeds,” Gay explains in his essay. “There is power — the hard architecture of institutions, coercion, money and command, the layer that can change in a season. There is ideology — the story a society tells about why those with power deserve it and why the rest should comply. And there is culture — the slow accumulation of everything a people has lived through, settled so deep that it is no longer argued but simply assumed. Most of our political commentary treats these as rival explanations: the institutionalist sees only power, the theorist only ideology, the culture critic only identity. Each is holding one limb of the animal.

“The reframe I would urge is this. Culture is not a third thing standing beside the other two. It is mostly the other two — power and ideology accumulated over generations and set hard, the way sediment is only the silt from yesteryear’s flood waters deposited over time, slowly compressing to a firmer sedimentary structure. What a people will accept, resist or demand today is the settled residue of the power arrangements and the justifying stories it absorbed long before anyone now living was old enough to question them. This is why culture is the slowest layer to move, and why, when it finally does move, power and ideology have no choice but to follow.”

Deep culture always returns to shape a society in a way similar to how a person’s emotional subconscious is forever biting at the heels of rational cognition. Culture is the substructure upon which the superstructure of ideology, politics and economics are built — the opposite of how modern thought would have it.

As political orders around the world enter a protracted period of upheaval, Gay’s frame of whether they are aligned or not with their cultural grounding is one of the more compelling paradigms for making sense of it all.

title: A New Dawn For Mathematical Progress
content:
Credits

Atoosa Kasirzadeh is a philosopher and mathematician. She is a research scientist at DeepMind Institute and an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University. Her research is focused on the social and scientific implications of AI.

In the past few months, unreleased frontier AI systems have significantly disrupted a classic conception of mathematics. They successfully established a [complete formalization](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem) of Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, [found a solution](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/) to the Navier-Stokes problem and — just a few days ago — generated [hundreds of manuscripts](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/) that each purport to prove an important mathematical problem. Most recently, on October 26, another of the Clay Millennium Prize problems was [felled](https://openai.com/index/building-scientific-understanding-with-academic-communities/) by an AI system.

Mathematicians reacted with a volatile mixture of optimism, anxiety and deep disorientation. In July, for example, Kirwin Hampshire, a Ph.D. student in mathematics, published an [essay](https://kirwinhampshire.substack.com/p/the-dark-night-of-mathematics) he titled “The Dark Night of Mathematics” in which he voiced the fear that human mathematicians might soon become obsolete next to AI systems with far greater speed and memory. “I am suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments,” he wrote. “I have been screaming internally for days. It feels as though I am living inside of a nightmare.” For Hampshire, the very act of _doing_ mathematics — the human struggle, the human aesthetic judgment, the human feeling and value of finding, understanding and sharing a new proof — could become a quaint artisanal craft, with human mathematicians no longer needed to push the frontier of mathematics.

Some mathematicians have realized that they must radically rethink their professional role and identity in light of this new technological reality. I was recently at an AI conference where a Fields Medal winner gave a talk on the frontier capabilities of AI systems for math problems. They closed their talk by saying: “We need to develop new theories of care and love.” This call was quite telling: a world-class mathematical theorist asking for theories of a very different kind. The mathematician, it seems, might become a philosopher of care and love. In a short essay, Logan Graves, a mathematical philosopher, [went further](https://logangraves.com/priest-monk-mathematician), suggesting that “the era of human mathematicians is ending, if not _ended_”; human mathematicians should find a new purpose in life, he wrote, and “the future of the human mathematical community, and eventually all scientific communities, is the practice of priests, then that of monks. Not researchers.”

Terence Tao, a prominent Fields Medal winner and mathematics professor, acknowledged the deep complexity of this historical moment. Adopting a cautiously optimistic stance, he [forecast](https://teorth.github.io/tao-web/slides/age-of-ai-icm-2026.pdf) that the mathematical “community will emerge stronger and more resilient than before.” Daniel Litt, a professor of mathematics at the University of Toronto, offered a set of core problems that should be solved for building the future of mathematics in an intriguing [essay](https://www.daniellitt.com/blog/2026/8/11/the-end-of-mathematics/) called “The End of Mathematics.” Litt wrote: “I’m broadly optimistic that mathematics will survive and flourish,” but that requires the mathematical community to address complex (not merely formal) questions such as redesigning institutions that incentivize high-quality scientific research and reorienting human capital.

Each of these reactions is entirely understandable; each represents a deeply respectable and admirable attempt to face and process a disruption to established ways of doing, being or becoming — of doing a certain type of mathematics and of being or becoming a particular type of mathematician.

Because these reactions respond to different dimensions of a complex concern, it is helpful to distinguish between four central questions that urgently need answers. First: What _is_ mathematical progress, and how is mathematics actually advanced? Second: How is the epistemic and creative agency of practicing mathematicians being disrupted? Third: How should we educate future human mathematicians and sustain human mathematical capacities? And fourth: How should incentives, research and structures for reward and credit be reorganized?

I start by distinguishing between two models of mathematical progress. I call them the _checklist model_ and the _generative encounter model_. In the checklist model, mathematical progress is primarily about incremental advancement in proving what humans, at a rather recent point in our history, have designated a checklist of “major mathematical problems.” The generative encounter model, on the other hand, conceptualizes mathematical progress as inherently open-ended and unfinished, and its development, for the time being, is subject to negotiation with definitions of human purpose, desire and experience.

> “Mathematics is one of the greatest things humans have built. Like all our built things, it keeps changing as we change — and our understanding of it keeps changing too.”

## **The Checklist Model**

Under the checklist model, mathematical progress consists of resolving well-defined, complex problems that are specified in advance. These include competition problems designed to measure the frontier of human mathematical capabilities such as those of the International Mathematical Olympiad, famous conjectures such as Fermat’s Last Theorem (or last conjecture), formalization benchmarks such as Freek Wiedijk’s list of 100 formalization challenges and prize problems such as Clay’s Millennium problems. Each of these can be considered an item on a checklist. Mathematical progress proceeds at rate at which the boxes get ticked, and reward and credit attribution goes to whoever ticks them first. This model of mathematical progress is attractive because it is neat and it makes progress easily measurable. That is why it underpins both the prestige economy of mathematics (Olympiad medals, the Fields Medal, the Millennium Prizes) and the benchmark culture of AI.

AI systems have been rapidly excelling at solving a checklist of major mathematical problems. Some mathematicians like [Tao](https://mathstodon.xyz/@tao/116477351524980995) refer to a new age of “proof post-scarcity” in which checklists of mathematical conjectures, including ones to be added in the future, are quickly proved or disproved one after the other by increasingly powerful AI systems.

A subset of the mathematical community has long organized its conception of progress around this model and the straightforward systems for reward and credit that it produces. Whoever solves a major problem from a canonical checklist earns the credit, and that cements their status as a genius (often a _lone_ genius, which is important). Entire research and academic institutions grew up around this incentive structure, and generations of students were taught that (one of) their highest aspirations should be to solve (at least) one of these problems. Now that AI systems can solve these problems, the norm that reserved such achievements exclusively for humans, and rewarded humans for them, no longer carries the social weight it once did. This means that, as Cornell mathematics professor Steven Strogatz said in a [recent interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LfGenpmOjDQ), the age of lone human mathematical heroes is over.

But the end of the lone human hero is not the end of human mathematicians.

AI is showing us that the incentives around the checklist model are not sustainable anymore. While loss and grief are valid responses to this new reality, remaining stuck there leaves the community unable to respond to radically transformative changes. We should look at this historical moment as an opportunity to redesign the structures that motivate and reward mathematical work, and we should do it soon.

> “AI brings us back to an old philosophical question: Where does mathematics come from?”

The checklist model rests on a remarkably narrow conception of mathematical inquiry. Even before AI systems started solving problems, the model didn’t seem to directly serve real-world problems. Many mathematicians have long worked in “exploratory mode,” disregarding questions about whether their lines of inquiry had any practical usefulness. G.H. Hardy, an English mathematician who died in 1947, is famous for writing “I have never done anything ‘useful.’ No discovery of mine has made, or is likely to make, directly or indirectly, for good or ill, the least difference to the amenity of the world.”

If mathematical progress is bound to the values of human mathematicians who can decide what to formalize, determine which problems truly matter, co-create with software and artificial agents and invent or discover novel domains of inquiry, then AI does not signal an end for the field. Instead, it opens a vast, unprecedented space of possibility.

The checklist model of mathematical progress is not representative of the actual progress in “mathematics” when we look at the history of the field. Under its narrow view, the pessimism of some mathematicians (_We are becoming obsolete_; _There is no need for future humans to do mathematics_; _No valuable rewards for doing mathematics remain for humans now_) offers no guidance about what mathematicians should do next.

Under a different model of mathematical progress, which I call the generative encounter model, proving major problems is just one piece of “doing mathematics” or “being a mathematician.” Here, AI’s impact on the mathematical community, generational education and institutional design is much more open to constructive and creative adjustment.

## **The Generative Encounter Model**

In 1939, George Dantzig [arrived](https://web.archive.org/web/20180421052355/http://rev-inv-ope.univ-paris1.fr/fileadmin/rev-inv-ope/files/26305//IO-26305-1.pdf) late to a statistics class during his doctoral studies at Berkeley and found two problems written on the blackboard. He thought they were homework assignments from the professor, Jerzy Neyman, so he solved them and handed in his work. “About six weeks later,” according to his own account, Dantzig and his wife “were awakened by someone banging on our front door. It was Neyman. He rushed in with papers in hand, all excited.” The problems weren’t homework, it turned out, but rather famous unsolved problems, and Neyman wanted to rush to publish Dantzig’s work.

After Berkeley, Dantzig became an adviser to the U.S. Air Force Comptroller. He [was tasked](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~gasarch/BLOGPAPERS/Albers-InterviewGeorgeB-1986.pdf) with finding a way to mechanize the planning and budgeting of the military’s staggering logistical operations. The reality he faced was one of worldly complexity. Thousands of human clerks were tasked with drafting and creating supply-chain and personnel schedules entirely by hand, using heuristic trial-and-error.

There were no preexisting mathematical problems for Dantzig to solve here. He faced the chaotic physical reality and had to figure out how to translate it into a useful mathematical abstraction. This is an example of an “encounter” in the generative encounter model: a social and practical problem with apparently little to do with “just proving” mathematics.

As Dantzig himself later recounted in an interview, the military used the word “program” — not computer code but rather a plan or a schedule. Dantzig’s goal, therefore, became simply to more rapidly develop a program for time-staged deployment, training and logistics. He was not trying to prove a theorem or conjecture; he was not hired for that, nor did he expect an award for developing such a thing. He was trying to fix an administrative bottleneck.

To do so, he invented (or discovered, if you like) a class of problems that needed solving. He did this by structuring and interpreting the situation into an elegant formulation composed of two distinct parts: a linear objective to be achieved (maximize efficiency or minimize cost, for example) and a set of constraints expressed as a system of linear inequalities (a certain number of planes, pilots, gallons of fuel, etc.). He called this mathematical package a “linear programming problem.” The word “programming” he borrowed directly from the military’s administrative vocabulary.

By mathematically separating the physical constraints from the ultimate goal and approximating both with linear relationships, Dantzig mapped a messy real-world problem onto a clean, high-dimensional geometric object: a convex polyhedron. This abstraction transformed a question of scheduling human action and materials into a question of geometry, and in doing so, made it a part of an open-ended conception of _mathematics_.

Dantzig had taste. He made a crucial recognition: As a matter of mathematical necessity, the optimal solution to a programming problem would lie on one of the vertices of a polyhedron. The search for the “best” mathematical solution or the best “schedule” thus became a search for the “highest” corner of a geometric object. Dantzig then developed the now-famous [simplex algorithm](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/87252.88081) to systematically search for that optimal vertex by efficiently moving along the edges of the polyhedron until reaching the peak.

![Image 1](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2026/10/image.jpeg?fm=pjpg&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=71f8abeabe15a5af1cea193153e9a974)

(Victor Treushchenko, Wikimedia)

Before Dantzig, there was no mathematical community of “linear programmers” listing out problems in their field and seeking to solve them. He _formed_ a community, one that grew to include operations researchers, mathematical economists and industrial engineers as additional sub-branches of the field were developed. This group defined itself by a shared interest in a set of problems that had not existed a decade earlier.

Linear programming works for continuous resources like gallons of fuel, but what if a problem demands whole units? You cannot fly half an airplane or assign a third of a pilot to a mission. That physical constraint, a new encounter, forced the invention of a branch of operations research known as [integer programming](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-11008-0). This, in turn, opened a vast new frontier of mathematics, generating entirely new branches of mathematics, theoretical models and novel algorithms, which themselves collided with new problems and produced yet more [fields](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0927050705801720?casa_token=LkcwtZ05fhAAAAAA:X_sSBsrLjS34Kc43dF9we5Flw1b_7NCGMABHx4D1LTJzFtFv2Nubjf1dRyIQ_GOcuHgDC8uB) of [inquiry](https://www.mheducation.co.uk/introduction-to-operations-research-2024-release-ise-9781266933226-emea-group).

> “A revolution in automated proof discovery, on its own, guarantees nothing definite about the future of mathematics, which remains an open-ended domain of inquiry.”

Before the MIT mathematician Norbert Wiener created the field we now call _cybernetics_, which later formed the backbone of modern artificial intelligence, he was confronted with a wartime problem similar in some ways to the one that faced Dantzig: how to shoot a plane out of the sky using an antiaircraft gun on the ground when the enemy pilot was taking evasive action. Aiming at the plane guaranteed a miss, so where do you aim? As Wiener later [put](https://direct.mit.edu/books/oa-monograph/4581/Cybernetics-or-Control-and-Communication-in-the) it, “It is exceedingly important to shoot the missile, not at the target, but in such a way that missile and target may come together in space at some time in the future. We must hence find some method of predicting the future position of the plane.” This problem was not on any checklist of mathematical problems. It had to be encountered.

Wiener’s move was to reframe the problem. He stopped treating a pilot as a strategic adversary to be outguessed and instead considered him a component in a system to be characterized. He saw that the pilot’s evasive maneuvers were not purely random; they were responses to the gunner’s actions and corrections against the aircraft’s physical lags. In this view, the gunner, the antiaircraft gun, the shell, the pilot and the aircraft all formed a single system with different feedback loops between them. To this loop Wiener added what he called a predictor.

In his 1948 book “[Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine](https://dn790006.ca.archive.org/0/items/norbert-wiener-cybernetics/Norbert_Wiener_Cybernetics_text.pdf),” Wiener described the task as designing a predictor whose characteristics “depend[ed] on a long-time acquaintance with the statistics of the ensemble of time series which we desire to predict.” In this sentence, the significance of real-world encounters for mathematical progress becomes quite obvious. The physical problem of gunnery was converted into a statistical problem about time. This conversion created a cluster of new mathematical problems: What is the optimal filter to separate a signal from noise? How can one best predict the future course of a random process from its past? What, formally, does it even mean for a system to be goal-directed?

The answers gave birth to the theory of statistical filtering and prediction and ultimately the feedback formalism that organized the new mathematics and science of cybernetics. Wiener created a new branch of mathematics for describing, explaining, understanding and predicting control and communication in both machines and living organisms. It generated a new community, a new field, which brought different epistemic stances together to better understand the world. The now-famous [Macy Conferences](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62246/chapter-abstract/550966038?redirectedFrom=fulltext) in the late 1940s and early 1950s brought together biologists, psychiatrists, anthropologists and engineers around a set of problems that previously had no disciplinary home. Cybernetics, as a new branch of mathematics, created a new home for such inquiries.

Most telling of all, the original purpose that sparked the work was soon superseded. Wiener’s antiaircraft predictor was not widely deployed; a simpler design from Bell Labs won the military contract. Had it been a problem on a checklist, Wiener’s project might be seen as a failure, seeing as how it was an inferior solution to another. But the mathematics it created survived and went on to reshape our understanding of many systems, from factory automation to human and artificial neural systems.

## **There Is No Distinction Between Pure And Applied Mathematics. There Is Only Mathematics.**

During my doctoral studies in mathematics (in the field of “operations research”), I attended a national conference for mathematical graduate students in Canada. The atmosphere was charged with a peculiar intellectual stratification between “pure” (or “real”) mathematics and “applied” mathematics.

When some of my peers, who were working on classical analytic number theory and variations of the Riemann hypothesis, learned that others of us were researching mathematical and computational approaches for large-scale decision problems, their response was immediate and dismissive: _What you do is not real mathematics._ To them, _real mathematical inquiry_ belonged exclusively to the solitary pursuit of proving major theorems within self-contained axiomatic systems. Not considered _real mathematics_ were efforts to develop and formulate algorithms to solve large-scale decision problems, optimize resource distribution, translate frictions and decision problems into mathematical structures, and perhaps find new theories of decision-making in real-world encounters.

The culture of mathematicians has for generations harbored a hidden hierarchy between these two communities of mathematicians: Generating abstract proofs supposedly constituted “real” mathematics whereas dealing with the messy, empirical world was dismissed as an inferior craft. Historically, this divide served a practical purpose: It functioned as a tool for creating an epistemic division of labor, organizing mathematical activity and giving rise to separate institutions, journals and reward structures for tackling a variety of different cognitive engagements with mathematical problems.

By placing the generation of proofs for very complex problems at the apex of this hierarchy, the pure-applied dichotomy, perhaps unintentionally, popularized the idea that pure mathematics is (real) mathematics. In doing so, it enshrined the checklist model of mathematical progress, leading many to mistake measuring a peculiar type of epistemic activity for the entirety of mathematical progress. The conflation of the title _mathematician_ with those who study only pure mathematics is a pervasive and uncritical cultural prejudice. It is one that relegates researchers who grapple with physical and systemic realities to second-class status. I think AI has forced us to correct that prejudice, and I do not think we can ignore it.

> “A true golden age of mathematics, rooted in human purpose and new visions of education and collective reward, may have just begun.”

Dantzig too faced gatekeeping by pure mathematicians, whose insistence that their work was the only “real” mathematics generated a highly exclusionary perception of the discipline. When asked whether he thought of himself as an operations researcher or a mathematician, Dantzig answered: “I consider myself a mathematician. I don’t differentiate between pure mathematics and applied mathematics. I know other people will tell you there is a difference, but there isn’t.”

When the interviewer noted that pure mathematicians often describe operations researchers as “second-rate mathematicians playing with toy problems,” Dantzig’s response was characteristically blunt: “Mathematicians are snobs.”

“Present company excepted,” the interviewer responded. “Pure math involves clean problems, but real-world problems are messy.”

“Real-world problems are all dirty, that’s correct,” Dantzig said. “Any model of them is an approximation of reality; it’s not reality.”

Dantzig’s experience in the development of linear programming led him to become a strong advocate of encountered problems as the inspiration for interesting and challenging mathematical work. Speaking to [Donald Albers](https://www.informs.org/Explore/History-of-O.R.-Excellence/Oral-Histories/George-Dantzig) in 1984, he said:

Just because my mathematics has its origin in a real problem doesn’t make it less interesting to me—just the other way around, I find it makes the puzzle I am working on all the more exciting. I get satisfaction out of knowing that I’m working on a relevant problem. I find that just as much mathematical ingenuity has to go into solving problems from a newly developing area as from some old so-called pure math area.

Operations research, Dantzig went on, is the “science of decision-making”: the art of “abstracting a problem and putting it into mathematical form.” For him, mathematical practice spans a continuous spectrum from the abstract theorist seeking formal solutions down to the practitioner needing an actionable answer to a concrete crisis. To chop this continuum in half and declare one end “noble” and the other “second-class” misses the entire dynamic essence of mathematical inquiry.

The “crisis” of AI’s ability to rapidly solve complex problems, and mathematicians’ responsibility for building infrastructure for mathematical inquiry in the near future, can be seen in a new light. A messy encounter with the world, after all, can be the birthplace of the purest mathematics, and pure mathematics can find its way back to the world.

## **Powerful Systems, Open Futures**

We must approach this historical moment with the utmost care. The main challenge is not only to mourn a loss. It is, more importantly, to build a better future. The development and deployment of AI is forcing us to redraw the maps of human motivation, reward and research prestige in mathematics. Redrawing those maps does not have to erase human agency — but it can if approached clumsily.

If we restructure how we assign credit, set research priorities and reward work — moving away from proof discovery alone — we can cultivate “Dantzig-style” mathematical thinkers. These are people who use AI to free their creative faculties and push into deeper, more interesting or more urgent territory.

This moment has opened a vast space of possibilities. New incentives can be designed around problems that genuinely matter for better human life, for individual and social health, for planetary flourishing. And we are not short of those problems.

Perhaps the mathematical community and its future generations can move from “_Who proved it?”_ to “_Who decided this was worth proving, why, and how did we make sure it was right?”_ Large collaborations already exist in mathematics: the Polymath projects, the Lean community’s Mathlib, the long effort to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem. Mathematicians can coordinate around shared goals that matter for their community, but also for the world.

They now need to scale coordination capabilities. But how?

I think the mathematical community must embrace the generative encounter model of mathematical progress. This requires that we treat the integration of AI in mathematics as a rich, independent subject of foundational analysis. Far from signaling the end of mathematics, this opens room for examining a vast frontier of urgent, encountered mathematical problems that require deep work, often in collaboration with other disciplines. Here are four critical clusters of mathematical problems where this work is urgently needed:

1.   **Provably safe cyber infrastructure**. [](https://iiasa.ac.at/blog/mar-2026/our-infrastructure-is-much-more-fragile-than-we-think?__cf_chl_tk=34GxwqBGZcUgfmbqZfNf8MV73IrUwBe1.ZNWwyWq8J4-1792792569-1.0.1.1-n2S6KM.Ag4QMPJ2HCm3lYf4.KZKqQoa3DMm_NhSudws)Our global digital systems remain profoundly [fragile.](https://iiasa.ac.at/blog/mar-2026/our-infrastructure-is-much-more-fragile-than-we-think?__cf_chl_tk=34GxwqBGZcUgfmbqZfNf8MV73IrUwBe1.ZNWwyWq8J4-1792792569-1.0.1.1-n2S6KM.Ag4QMPJ2HCm3lYf4.KZKqQoa3DMm_NhSudws) Human mathematicians, using AI as a high-throughput collaborative partner, can work to find the flaws and rebuild our cyber foundations from first principles, establishing provably secure and mathematically verified computing environments.
2.   **The epistemic mechanics of deep learning**. [](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.16496)Our mathematical grasp of how neural networks learn, generalize and represent high-dimensional data is still in its [infancy.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.16496) Several concerns about advanced AI causing catastrophic harm originate directly from this gap in understanding. Despite significant advances, developing a rigorous “mathematical science of deep learning” remains a fundamental challenge, and solving it is a precondition for building truly trustworthy systems.
3.   **The mathematics of multi-agent control**. The dynamic alignment or misalignment of interacting, agentic AI systems remains [poorly understood](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.14143). We need to draw on mathematical disciplines such as mathematical security, safety engineering, robust mechanism design and game theory to analyze how individually optimized agents behave when they coordinate, compete or collide.
4.   **The epistemology of machine-generated proofs**. What should we do with AI-generated “proofs” that are too long, too complex, or too alien for human minds to [understand or verify](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02822-9)? Rather than rejecting them because they are unintelligible, we must develop new mathematical techniques for explanation, logical translation and interactive verification that make them understandable. We shouldn’t rush to rely on such proofs, but these techniques can give us reliable paths for turning raw automated output into genuine human understanding.

None of these problems appear on a checklist of mathematical problems. None of them will be easily “solved” by a single human mathematician. Each needs teams of humans equipped with technological tools to decide what and how to formalize and interpret mathematical problems that matter —and how to build institutions to apply the offered solutions.

The world around us is human-made: the buildings, the networks, the institutions, the AI models themselves. Mathematics is one of the greatest things humans have built. Like all our built things, it keeps changing as we change — and our understanding of it keeps changing too.

This brings us back to an old philosophical question: Where does mathematics come from? The cognitive scientists George Lakoff and Rafael Núñez gave one answer in their book “[Where Mathematics Comes From](https://pages.ucsd.edu/~rnunez/COGS252_Readings/Preface_Intro.PDF)”: embodied human cognition. [Platonists](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/platonism-mathematics/) give another: Mathematics is discovered, not made. Its objects exist independently of humans, and mathematicians are explorers of a terrain that has been there all along and will still be there in the absence of any human. [Formalists](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/formalism-mathematics/) give a third response: Mathematics is a game of symbols and rules, and it is “true” only in the sense that a legal chess move is correct. I won’t settle the debate here. But every answer locates at least part of the origin of mathematics in an encounter: between minds and the world, between us and Plato’s heaven, or between human communities and the questions they find worth asking and answering. AI systems have now become a serious participant in that encounter.

A revolution in automated proof discovery, on its own, guarantees nothing definite about the future of mathematics, which remains an open-ended domain of inquiry. That future will be shaped not only by AIs but also by the preconditions that make doing mathematics possible, or impossible: the purposes, infrastructure and institutions we build around the questions we find worth asking and answering. These include how to verify results, how to assign credit, how to train students, how to value human cognition and agency, how to support those harmed by this transition and give them new systems of recognition to rely on, how to advance human and planetary flourishing, how to make tools and infrastructure broadly accessible and who sits at the table when these questions are answered.

Answering these questions requires science and mathematics as necessary elements of the sociotechnical foundation for a better future. And that we do not yet have.

> “New incentives can be designed around problems that genuinely matter for better human life, for individual and social health, for planetary flourishing. And we are not short of those problems.”

Viewed from the generative encounter model of mathematical progress, a true golden age of mathematics, rooted in human purpose and new visions of education and collective reward, may have just begun.

Suppose this situation and these questions are only temporary. What about later? What if we eventually build artificial superintelligence — systems that don’t just prove theorems but pose questions, judge which ones matter, design curricula and decide how rewards are distributed? Systems that automate the whole process of generative encounters?

The deepest version of the worry some “pure” mathematicians are articulating is not whether AI can automate mathematical proofs. It is whether AI eventually automates human purpose itself. But let’s not forget how we arrived here.

Our current moment is, among other things, a long-term consequence of the dream of formalizing mathematics, from the well-posed formulas of mathematical logic that gave rise to software engineering to the contemporary drive in the Lean community to formalize mathematics in machine-readable form so that machines might verify and, one day, prove or solve problems. In some sense, where we are today is partly the realization of a long dream held by a portion of the mathematical community. But living in a realized dream requires us to think carefully not just about the dream itself, but about its consequences. Purpose matters.

Whether the day ever comes when human purpose is fully automated none of us can know. But what is clear is that the future is shaped by what we dream and build today, and we owe it to ourselves, our children and future generations to dream and build it with care. In the end, the transition to the future is not separate from the future. And the transition is where the future is actually lived, dreamed and made.

_Author’s note: Thanks to Jim Brown, Marcus Hutter and Shane Legg for comments on this essay._

title: Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law
content:
Credits

MUNICH —Shortly after wandering into the Munich Urban Colab this summer, I found myself trying to follow an intense conversation in German about the city’s new experiment with autonomous buses. A local official, clocking my curious puzzlement, offered an aside in English: “We are asking ourselves: ‘What does it mean when the law is an experiment too?’”

No question may be more essential to governance in our era of dangerous uncertainty.

Global warming is accelerating faster than global treaties on mitigation can be negotiated. Climate catastrophes occur with a sudden ferocity beyond what current adaptation laws anticipate. Biological threats surface and kill before public health responses can be formulated. And AI is evolving faster and more wildly than regulators or lawmakers, or even its designers, expect.

All this dizzying unpredictability is undermining traditional legal structures. The threat is not just to the rule of law, but to the very nature of law, at least as humans have conceived it.

Our societies have long considered the law a slow and steady force, “the essential foundation of stability and order” in the words of J. William Fulbright. To that end, law is backward-looking — “the government of the living by the dead,” according to Oliver Wendell Holmes. The lawmaking process in republics and democracies is age-old: observe a problem, study its particularities, debate solutions and then carve out a rule that will endure for years or decades.

But what happens when the future arrives faster than your regional regulator or local parliament can make a rule?

The emerging answer is experimental law or, in Germany, where Munich is a hotbed, _Experimentierklauseln_. “Experimental clauses” refer to sections and parts of laws that are made flexible, often for set time periods, to allow for real-time adaptation or alteration in response to changing threats, climate or technology.

The shift toward such experimentation has begun, albeit slowly, in only certain areas of the law. Contract law and administrative law, especially where they touch on technology or other advanced sectors of the economy, are becoming more fluid.

Contracts, once used to protect against all contingencies, are now written more openly — explicitly anticipating new knowledge and adjustments. Among startups and innovation-oriented companies, written agreements are less likely to specify payments for specific work at specific times and more likely to establish processes for collaboration and shared decision-making.

For example, start-ups use [Agile contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agile_contracts) with vendors that, instead of pledging a final digital product at a price, set parameters of a creative process involving a test phase, iterative feedback loops and product benchmarks. Biotech startups rely on a “relational contract” with manufacturers to create a collaboration framework that includes regular meetings, shared lab notes and a commitment to use best efforts to scale a prototype.

Meanwhile, smart contracts have become commonplace in supply chains to allow for real-time changes in inventory levels. [Union contracts in digital workplaces](https://laborcenter.berkeley.edu/negotiating-tech/foundational-technology-rights/examples-of-technological-change-agreements/) often incorporate adaptive provisions — “continuous bargaining” in 21st-century labor parlance — with guidelines for how workers participate across the lifecycles of systems and products.

Modern tech procurement uses what’s called “Dynamic Service Level Agreements” that feature automatic updates, scalable license adjustments, and continuous remote monitoring and interventions by seller and buyer. “Data Processing Agreements” within cloud contracts dynamically adjust data handling and security protocols as privacy regulations and digital risks shift. In some cases, AI agents have [written contracts in code](https://www.adr.org/podcasts/ai-and-the-future-of-law/how-ai-is-changing-contract-law-with-dave-hoffman/) rather than in English. Put simply, some contracts now write themselves.

Similarly, regulatory agencies and public administrations have [moved away](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/01/17/good-act-transparency-federal-guidance-regulations/) from the time-consuming traditional rulemaking process, since rules quickly become outdated in a world so strange and fast-changing. Instead, agencies and administrative judges, particularly in advanced economies, are more likely to offer “guidance” — advisories, memos, letters or protocols that are regularly tweaked or edited in response to updated knowledge and changing circumstances.

These shifts point toward an emerging and quite radical recognition, especially in law, that extreme uncertainty is not a problem to be solved, but a reality and even an ally. The fact that the future is too hard for anyone to know is leveling. The regulator, the regulated and the everyday person all know the same thing: almost nothing.

The act of lawmaking then becomes a great collaboration between governments and experts and firms and workers and the regular people most affected. And that collaboration is a search, never-ending, for improvements and innovations and solutions.

Such collaboration turns lawmaking as we know it on its head. Implementation is required first to understand what the policy should be. In this new paradigm, resilience is grounded in fragility. Resilience does not come from buffering organizations against known risks, but by designing them to show quickly when they are broken, so they can be reconfigured. It is a kind of deliberately induced and carefully controlled institutional fragility. Strain is immediately apparent, triggering investigation and countermeasures well before it ramifies into catastrophe.

> “Experimental clauses allow for real-time adaptation in response to changing threats, climate or technology.”

## Climate Changes The Law

The stakes of achieving this new, more open mentality are expressed perhaps most clearly in our response to global warming. In the 2022 book, “Fixing the Climate: Strategies for an Uncertain World,” Columbia Law School’s Charles F. Sabel and UC San Diego’s David G. Victor argue that decades of top-down global climate diplomacy — from the Kyoto Protocol to the Paris Agreement — have failed because they rely on inflexible global treaties.

Treaties are among the oldest forms of law. But climate treaties are outdated the moment they are signed, because the climate is changing too quickly. And they don’t reflect the reality that climate change impacts — and opportunities to mitigate and adapt to climate change — are very different depending on location and context. (Sea level rise is not an issue in Mongolia; glacial melting does not plague Phoenix). The only viable way to make law and government is thus through relentless, highly structured and broadly collaborative local experimentation. This model, they noted, is neither “top down” nor “bottom up” but both at the same time.

“Our central aim is to reorient our current climate change regime away from failed efforts based on ex ante global consensus, and toward a system anchored in local and sectoral experimentalism and learning,” they [wrote](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691224558/fixing-the-climate?srsltid=AU7gw4W4fhfyWvN71QMBpUlAOwrqdmJCJRLjjSEPyCd2l_46mQFlWuWk).

This local experimentalist mindset is emerging especially in the metro regions of countries that have advanced economies and histories of collaborative lawmaking and regulation.

Two places that best fit that description are Singapore, which was built on deep cooperation between government technocrats and industry, and Germany’s bigger cities.

Experimental law first emerged in West Germany during the 1950s as a pragmatic mechanism for the Länder, or states, to exploit their autonomy under the 1949 Basic Law. Faced with ideological divisions and a lack of national precedent for building a post-authoritarian society, municipal and state agencies used “trial clauses” to break legacy rules on welfare, housing and local administrative reorganizations without setting precedents or locking local governments into long-term mandates. The first official _Experimentierklauseln_ allowed public schools to violate rigid curricular and education standards and test pedagogies, grading systems and models of comprehensive schools.

Experimental clauses fell out of fashion in the late 20th century but were revived for new challenges in the 21st century. In 2008, the Upper Saxony town of [Bohmte, Germany](https://www.csmonitor.com/World/Europe/2008/0912/p07s03-woeu.html), used an experimental clause to do something otherwise illegal: eradicate traffic lanes, street lines, traffic lights and stop signs to combat chronic speeding, utilizing a Dutch idea called [shared space](https://www.pps.org/article/shared-space).

Over the last decade, climate change and advances in technology and transportation inspired so much local experimentalism that the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action issued an official “Guide for Formulating Experimentation Clauses” in 2024. The guide runs 34 pages but contains three main rules: All experimental clauses must have an expiration date, a clear geographical or sectoral boundary, and rigorous evaluation.

Ask the federal ministry staff for a signature example, and you’ll hear about a Hamburg hospital that couldn’t get cancer tissue samples to a laboratory in time because of city traffic. The hospital wanted to use a drone instead, but German aviation regulations strictly forbid drones from flying “beyond the visual line of sight” of their operators over settled urban areas.

Instead of waiting years for federal airspace reform, Hamburg relied on experimental clauses to deviate from the federal Air Traffic Act for 18 months. During that time, the city-state established the U-Space Sandbox, a 30-square-kilometer experimental airspace over the Port of Hamburg.

Officials of the local and national governments worked with two German companies, Droniq and DFS Deutsche Flugsicheruntegration, to test the integration of drones with manned aviation. The experimentation eventually produced guidance and rules for a drone air traffic system, which are being incorporated into drafts of Germany’s federal U-Space Act.

> “Climate treaties are outdated the moment they are signed, because the climate is changing too quickly.”

## Living With Experimental Law

In Munich, I spent an evening inside one product of experimental law: an unusual new house at Goerzerstrasse 128, in the southeast neighborhood of Giesing. Munich, like so many cities, suffers from high housing prices and rents. The city held a competition for alternative solutions, and a self-organized housing syndicate won. It then used experimental clauses to deviate from strict German building codes.

The building was constructed with simple wood and cheap corrugated iron — what residents call “Favela-style” — and operates internally as a massive “shed flat.” The design is energy-efficient, and the roof captures rainwater in an underground cistern and feeds it directly back into the local groundwater table to combat drought.

The cost exceeded 3 million euros, drawn from public subsidies and private loans. But that’s cheap, given its scale. For now, 14 people — 13 adults and a six-year-old — share the open architecture, with frequent visitors. (A rock band was just leaving as I arrived.) The building is designed so it could be divided into at least nine separate apartments. While one-bedroom apartments in Munich rent for 1,700 euros a month, rent at Gorzer 128 is about 460 euros per person.

Gorzer 128 and other experiments helped inspire a national experimental clause called “Construction Turbo” (Section 246e of the German Federal Building Code), which allows municipalities to bypass existing planning standards until the end of 2030. The only unhappiness has come from neighbors who don’t like the building’s appearance (a jumble of metal and wood, quite different than the single-family craftsman homes on the street) and have been slow to engage with residents. Experimental law offers no cure for NIMBYism, at least not yet.

Beyond Gorzer 128, Munich’s experimental laws are most associated with efforts to transform streetscapes. A signal success is on the Kolumbusstraße, which a few years ago was a standard urban artery, lined with 120 concrete parking slots and choked with traffic.

Oliver May-Beckmann, who leads the MCube mobility cluster at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), says his group used an experimental clause to close the street to traffic for six months to create a Sommerstraße (Summer Street). Some drivers and residents complained to local officials. But because the project was a temporary and science-driven _Reallabor_, or real-world laboratory, politicians could push responsibility onto May-Beckmann and the scientists. “They’d say, ‘It’s just an experiment, let’s wait for the data,” he recalls.

For half a year _,_ Kolumbusstraße became a green space where children could play, residents could spend time and new forms of mobility were tested. The transformation was deliberately temporary, and after six months, the street returned to its previous state. But the evaluation produced a striking result: 66% of residents supported making the changes permanent. Whether and how to turn the experiment into a lasting transformation is now a decision for the City of Munich.

MCube also used an experimental clause to test a car-sharing strategy in Nymphenburg, an affluent neighborhood that houses Munich’s botanical garden. For 20 years, Germany’s car industry — BMW, Mercedes, Sixt — had been testing different forms of free-floating vehicle-sharing to try to cut emissions, but it just put more cars on the street because people used shared vehicles on top of their own. In MCube’s test, 10 local families gave up their private cars for 18 months, and MCube bought five electric cars, plugged into charging stations in an underground garage, for the families to share. It was a closed group — the sharing was just between the 10 households, and you knew who had the car before you.

The families communicated with each other and shared the cars well. MCube also discovered that when people know a car is always nearby, they were willing to pay significantly more in regular payments for access than they would pay with one-off models. MCube is now working with both BMW and Sixt, the Bavaria-based rental car company, to spread the model around Germany. The experimental clause is still in effect and is being used to test alternative car-sharing models in three other Munich neighborhoods.

Experimental clauses offer flexibility but demand deep collaboration with business, governments and everyday people, May-Beckmann says. Take [MINGA](https://muenchenunterwegs.de/minga), a new project that plans to put autonomous buses on Munich’s streets this fall. (Minga is both the name for Munich in the Bavarian dialect and an acronym for Münchens Automatisierter Integrations-Nahverkehr mit Gesellschaftlicher Akzeptanz, or “Munich Automated Public Transport with Ridepooling, Solo Bus and Bus Platoons.”

The project, which uses driverless vehicles without a set schedule or route, is enabled by experimental clauses derived from 2021 amendments to Section 1i of the German Road Traffic Act. The German government is providing 13 million euros in funds. MAN, a German commercial vehicle manufacturer, built the buses. Technical University of Munich scientists have worked on the software, the public transport administration is preparing to run the buses, and the city of Munich plans to operate the service for two years under experimental clauses and then evaluate it. Finally, it requires people to sign up, primarily to bridge the “first-mile/last-mile” gap of getting people to public transit hubs.

Experimental clauses, at their best, create space and permission for systems integration. That’s nearly impossible in conventional governance, where decisions are made sequentially, and services and programs are added one by one.

“Our goal is transferring knowledge into prototypes and bringing those into real life,” says May-Beckmann. “It’s crucial in Europe that mobility innovation isn’t just about a new car; it’s about a system. How do you integrate autonomous driving, city development, climate change and energy? We get funding to have industry and public administration work for us as a system.”

> “All experimental clauses must have an expiration date, a clear geographical or sectoral boundary, and rigorous evaluation.”

## Experiments In Sunshine & Medicine

The desire to experiment with law is not exclusively German. Barcelona placed the 22@ Innovation District under experimental law to test drones. In the UK, Bethesda and other Welsh cities have employed experimental clauses for “[Sunshine Tariffs](https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/article/energy-firm-to-take-control-of-household-appliances-pd2lkg72q)” to encourage renewable energy use. South Korea carved out an experimental exception in its transportation laws to install a hydrogen-powered mobility system in Gyeongsangbuk-do. In Japan, the experimental mantle is carried by the “Future Design” movement, where citizens in towns like Yahaba wear differently colored robes to design infrastructure plans for future generations.

If democracy doesn’t have to be part of the legal equation, then East Asia might be the world’s leader. Singapore, the world leader in temporary regulations, has built a financial powerhouse by permitting banking and fintech experiments for decades. More recently, it has been applying experimentalism to medicine. An [ongoing Health Sciences Authority experiment](https://www.arqon.com/post/singapore-hsa-opens-consultation-on-ai-samd-regulatory-sandbox) allows low- to medium-risk AI medical software to be used in public hospitals before formal registration. If the AI performs well for 12 months under clinician oversight, it can get an accelerated pathway to permanent approval.

More broadly, China and India have survived and prospered during rapid transitions by making experimentation a foundational principle of governance, often at the municipal or provincial levels.

In his 2024 book “Experimentalist Constitutions,” Peking University legal scholar Yueduan Wang details the Chinese government’s use of “experimental zones” to deviate from national law. In several areas, including green energy and mobility, municipalities have explicit legislative permission to try things. For example, the Shenzhen People’s Congress passed the 2025-2026 “Decision on Amending the Regulations of Shenzhen Special Economic Zone on Intelligent Connected Vehicles,” which allows fully driverless commercial taxis to bypass national safety standards.

India has embedded what it calls “regulatory sandbox” clauses directly into legislative updates. The Telecommunication Act of 2023 explicitly created a live testing environment that exempts companies from standard licensing fees to test 6G internet. Gujarat, where Narendra Modi served as chief before becoming national prime minister, is an epicenter of experimentation. It houses India’s first operational “smart city,” Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), between Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar, to test flexible financial regulations. Many of its startups use an “interoperable sandbox” to temporarily bypass rules on corporate governance, liquidity, capital minimums, reporting timelines and marketing as they test hybrid fintech products.

## Experimental Enough For AI?

Despite successes in fintech, mobility and housing, it is unclear whether experimental law will be fast or flexible enough for the ethereal, borderless realm of artificial intelligence.

In Germany, companies working with AI complain that experimental law remained too slow and earthbound to keep up. Ironically, they blame the European Union’s attempts to “lead” on experimental law and AI for the failure.

In 2024, the EU embraced experimental law with its landmark AI Act. Article 57 of the AI Act included an explicit mandate for experimental law — every member state was required to establish at least one national “AI regulatory sandbox” by August 2026. But the mandate made the program politically divisive within several countries. In a dozen member states, including Germany and France, governments couldn’t even agree on which national agency or authority would establish their sandbox. The EU acknowledged the dysfunction this summer, pushing the deadline for a national AI mandate back a year to August 2027, via the [AI Omnibus](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ai-omnibus-enters-force).

Few in Europe’s AI policymaking community expect to meet that deadline. The trouble goes beyond the EU’s slow bureaucracy. It’s hard to employ experimental law when you’re terrified of real impacts and results. Notably, the AI Act doesn’t require experimental deployment of AI regulation in the real world. As a result, those nations that are moving toward an AI regulatory sandbox are limiting experiments to theoretical exercises or purely legal assessments. But it’s impossible to create experimental laws for AI in the real world if you won’t experiment with AI in the real world.

In Munich, Till Klein, head of regulation at the non-profit “appliedAI Institute for Europe,” says that regulatory sandboxes that do exist for AI simply have too many restrictions to be useful. “Policymakers act like sandboxes will fix all the new rules,” says Klein. “But a sandbox is more like a sniper rifle than a shotgun; your experiment has to be precise for it to be meaningful.”

His colleague Demian Niemeyer, a lawyer and senior AI regulatory expert at appliedAI, sees the choke point as cultural. “People trained in law here are trained in a ‘Bismarck mindset,’” he says. “They are incredibly risk-averse. If you want to make something better and understand risks, you need a trial-and-error mindset.”

The paradox is that fear of applying experimental law to AI has left AI running free, well beyond law and regulation. Another fear also hamstrings experimental law: fear of regulatory capture.

That’s understandable, since effective experimental law requires regulators to collaborate closely with companies and stakeholders. Experimental law challenges the conception of regulation and law as walls between the watcher and the watched.

> “The paradox is that fear of applying experimental law to AI has left AI running free, well beyond law and regulation.”

In 2024 and 2025, fear of capture stirred controversy and delayed the drafting of Germany’s federal Reallabore-Gesetz (Regulatory Sandboxes) Act, an attempt to go beyond experimental clauses on particular subjects and create a broader framework for experimental law.

The Social Democrats, left-wing groups and some scholars argue that broad authorization of experimental clauses risks turning into backdoor-lobbying channels for Big Tech and powerful corporations seeking exemptions from labor, safety and privacy laws. Most of the objections were AI-focused.

In response, the proposed law’s backers incorporated _regulatorisches Lernen_ (regulatory learning) as a sandbox objective. When a project is approved under an experimental clause, the outcomes cannot remain hidden. The law requires continuous evaluation of the testing, and the resulting insights must be reported transparently. There are limited exclusions for genuine intellectual property.

The law also seeks to avoid narrow regulatory discussions between a company and a government agency via a “Regulatory Sandboxes Innovation Portal.” The portal is supposed to facilitate broad co-creation of law by connecting stakeholders from business, academia, public administration and civil society.

The legislation, renamed the Bundeserprobungsgesetz (Federal Proving Act), passed the Bundestag in late June. A second legislative body, the Bundesrat, would formally enact it as law in September. At the Munich Urban Colab, the immediate reaction was uncertainty. People would have to experiment with the new law and see.
